Timing the break-up of the Baltica and Laurentia connection in Nuna –
Rapid plate motion oscillation and plate tectonics in the Mesoproterozoic
J. Salminena,b, S.-Å. Elmingc, P. Layerd
aGeological Survey of Finland, P.O. Box 96, FI-02151 Espoo, Finland
bDepartment of Geosciences and Geography, P.O. Box 64, FI-00014 University of Helsinki, Finland
cDepartment of Civil, Environmental and Natural Resources Engineering, Luleå University of Technology, 97187 Luleå, Sweden
dGeophysical Institute and Department of Geosciences, University of Alaska Fairbanks, Fairbanks, AK 99775, USA
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: Meso– to Neoproterozoic geological and paleomagnetic data support a direct connection between Baltica and
Paleomagnetism Laurentia in both Nuna and Rodinia supercontinents, however in different relative configurations. Previous
40Ar-39Ar geochronology paleomagnetic data limit the time of break-up of Nuna core configuration and ca. 90◦rotation of Baltica relative
Baltica
to Laurentia between 1.27 Ga and 0.99 Ga. Despite the well documented relative motion of continents, the
Nuna
tectonic mode during the Meso– to Neoproterozoic has been questioned and the operation of single lid tectonics
NENA
at 1.6–1.0 Ga during the Nuna-Rodinia supercontinent cycles has been proposed.
Drift velocities
Inertial interchange true polar wander In this study, new paleomagnetic and whole rock 40Ar-39Ar geochronological data from a basic dyke in Stugun
central Sweden are combined with coeval data to produce a 1.22 Ga (1.244–1.200 Ga) moderate-quality
paleomagnetic pole. This is done to better estimate the break-up time of the core of Nuna and explore the
plate tectonics at the Mesoproterozoic. The new pole fills part of the 1.247–1.140 Ga gap in the paleomagnetic
record of Baltica. By comparing apparent polar wander paths (APWPs) and calculated drift velocities, a break-up
of Baltica and Laurentia at 1.12–1.04 Ga is suggested. Plate velocities calculated for Laurentia, Baltica and
Siberia for the time of the Nuna supercycle are similar and low to moderately high corresponding with the
present-day tectonic speeds. Furthermore, the obtained velocity peaks may be related with onset of the break-up
of the Nuna supercontinent, the break-up of the direct Baltica–Laurentia connection in Nuna and nascent
Rodinia. We suggest that the velocity peaks and large oscillating shifts in late Mesoproterozoic pole positions for
Laurentia and Baltica result from a combination of relative plate motion and inertial interchange true polar
wander (IITPW) events. Both IITPW events and relative plate motions argue for an operation of plate tectonics in
the Meso– to Neoproterozoic.

for the mean direction. Plat/Plon, paleolatitude/paleolongitude of the pole. A95, Radius of the 95% confidence cone of the pole. Age, radiometric ages for the studied
rock: **Whole rock 40Ar/39Ar, *** U-Pb baddeleyite. R, updated Van der Voo criteria (Meert et al., 2020). * indicates the site means used for the calculation of the
mean pole.

Numbers – ages in Ma.
Baltica falls in between the ~ 1.25 Ga grand mean pole for the J¨amtland
complex and the ~ 1.05 Ga pole of Laanila–Ristija¨rvi dykes (Mertanen
et al., 1996) forming an younging equatorial eastward trend from ca.
1.25 to 1.05 Ga (Fig. 8). Two poles, the ca.1.12 Ga Salla dyke pole
(Salminen et al., 2009) and the ca.1.14 Ga pole determined from the
Keurusselka¨ impact structure (Table 3), deviate from this trend and plot
at high latitudinal positions creating a hairpin with 80–95◦ loop be-
tween the 1.22 and 1.05 Ga poles. The Salla dyke pole is a high quality
B–grade pole (Evans et al., 2021) with a proven primary magnetization,
but since the pole is of only one dyke intrusion secular variation may not
have been averaged out (Salminen et al., 2009). However, the width of
the Salla dyke is up to 170 m and cooling of the dyke is not instanta-
neous. For the lower quality pole from the Keurusselka¨ impact structure
a positive impact test has been demonstrated (Pesonen, 2001), which is
analogous to the baked contact test, however, also for this pole secular
variation may not have been averaged out (Raiskila et al., 2011).
Because of the possibility that secular variation are not averaged out for
the 1.14–1.12 Ga poles, we explore two options for post–1.22 Ga
apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Baltica. In the APWP option A
the 1.14 Ga Keurusselka¨ and 1.12 Ga Salla poles are included, and the
path makes a 80–95◦hairpin loop to high latitudes at 1.14–1.12 Ga and
in the APWP option B the 1.14–1.12 Ga poles are neglected and the path
follows an eastward younging trend on equatorial latitudes from 1.25 to
1.05 Ga (Fig. 8). These two options have different implications for the
timing of the relative ~ 90◦ clockwise rotation of Baltica to Laurentia
(Patchett et al., 1978; Piper, 1980; Pesonen and Neuvonen, 1981;
Cawood et al., 2010; Cawood and Pisarevsky, 2017) during the transi-
tion from Nuna to the Rodinia supercontinent and will be further dis-
Fig. 8. The new pole of this study and 1.7–0.9 Ga high quality paleomagnetic cussed in the following chapters.
poles for Baltica (Table 3). Two APWP options for Baltica are explored. Arrows
points from older to younger paleopoles.

Code, code used in Figs. 8, 9, 12, 13. Rockname, name of the rock unit. Slat/Slong, Latitude/longitude of sampling site. Age, isotope age results. Method: a =APWP, c =39Ar(cid:0) 40Ar, d =K(cid:0) Ar, e =Rb(cid:0) Sr (mineral
isochron), f =Rb(cid:0) Sr (whole rock), g =U(cid:0) Pb, h =Sm(cid:0) Nd, j =Pb(cid:0) Pb, k =Lu(cid:0) Hf, s =stratigraphic, corr. =correlation, int. =interpolated. Nominal age, Mean of several age determinations or the one favored by pole
authors. Pol, polarity of the isolated magnetization direction. N/R/C/M, normal/reversed/combined/mixed polarity. B/N, number of sites/samples. D, declination. I, inclination. alpha95, the radius of the 95% confidence
cone in Fisher (1953) statistics. Plat/Plong, paleolatitude/paleolongitude of the pole. A95, radius of the 95% confidence cone of the pole. Key, Grade of the pole (Pesonen et al., 1991; Evans et al., 2021). Greenland rotated
to Laurentia reference frame using Euler parameters (67.5 , 241.5 , 013.8) from Roest and Srivastava (1989). * in pole indicates that the Greenland pole is rotated to Laurentia.

On basis of the two options of APWP for Baltica two models of the 1.11–1.09 Ga for Laurentia (see also Swanson-Hysell et al., 2019) and
20–50 cm/yr for Baltica at 0.95–0.92 Ga (see also Salminen et al.,
2021b) are obtained. The late Mesoproterozoic peak velocities of Lau-
rentia correlate temporally with the earlier stages of the Grenvillian
orogeny. Swanson-Hysell et al. (2019) proposed that the rapid subduc-
tion during the orogeny led to collisional orogens along the leading
margin of Laurentia during the formation of Rodinia. Elevated velocities
for Siberia at 1.05–1.00 Ga are comparable with the velocities of Lau-
rentia supporting a joint drift history of Siberia and Laurentia until the
Rodinia cycle (Evans and Mitchell, 2011; Ernst et al., 2016; Evans et al.,
2016). Early Neoproterozoic peak velocities of Baltica correlate
temporally with the final stages of the Sveconorwegian orogen. We
suggest that the similarity in velocities for the core continents, velocities
typical for modern day plate tectonics (Meert et al., 1993; Zahirovic
et al., 2015) provides an additional support for the joint history of
Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia at 1.75–1.11 Ga. The velocities also
indicate a break-up of NENA after 1.11 Ga and support the operation of
plate tectonics during the Paleo– to Mesoproterozoic.
We explored the high velocity by testing the effect of pole binning on
the calculated velocities using 50 Ma age bins for intervals with velocity
peaks. Such intervals are for Laurentia at 1.50–1.40 Ga and 1.15–1.05
Ga, Siberia at 1.05–1.00 Ga and Baltica at 0.95–0.90 Ga. In common for
these intervals are small age differences between poles, sometimes of
shifting quality, plotting at varying positions, which result in high ve-
locities, often with big error bars. By calculating mean pole positions for
50 Ma age intervals, the suspect high velocities are substituted by
calculated velocities that are dramatically lower (Fig. 11, Supplemen-
tary Table S1).

combination of rapid plate tectonics and TPW.
TPW may be recognized from coeval oscillations of poles along the
same great circle, however relative plate motions may obscure this TPW
signal (Evans, 2003). Here we are exploring the possible oscillations of
the paleomagnetic poles during the transition from the Nuna supercycle
to the Rodinia supercycle (Fig. 12). For this, we rotated the high-quality
paleopoles of Baltica, Siberia, India and Kalahari into their relative
configuration in the chosen Nuna and Rodinia supercontinents (Fig. 13).
Since Laurentia is in a central position in both supercontinents (e.g.,
Elming et al., 2021; Evans, 2021; Swanson-Hysell, 2021), the poles and
reconstructions are shown in the reference frame of Laurentia. Poles of
Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia show a common oscillating APWP path
during the tenure and initial break-up of Nuna at 1.64–1.24 Ga with
maximum swath length of 40◦. In addition, typical plate tectonic ve-
locities (4–12 cm/yr) are obtained for this interval (Fig. 11). A large
swath of ~ 70◦ along the Logan Loop of Laurentia is obtained for the
poles of Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia between 1.24 and 1.21 Ga and
1.14–1.12 Ga. For this interval, high plate velocities atypical for plate
tectonics are also obtained (Fig. 11) and these are interpreted to indicate
a TPW events (e.g., Evans, 2003; Swanson-Hysell et al., 2019). After
1.12 Ga the APWP of Baltica diverge from that of Laurentia +Siberia
indicating a change and the break-up of NENA. Large shifts in APWPs
are obtained during the nascent Rodinia in-between 1.12 Ga and ca.
1.05–1.04 Ga when APWPs of both Baltica and combined Laurentia +
Siberia show ca. 60◦–95◦ swathes (Fig. 12). When rotating the poles
relative to the positions of the continents in the Rodinia configuration,
the ca. 1.14–1.12 Ga poles are far apart, while the ca. 1.05–1.04 Ga poles
of Baltica and Laurentia +Siberia overlap, indicating separate drift of
these continents in between ca. 1.12 and1.05 Ga. In Rodinia configu-
ration, the 1.05–0.92 Ga poles of Baltica and Siberia oscillate along the
same great circle path defined by the 1.11–1.02 Ga poles of Laurentia
(Fig. 13). The oscillation of APWPs of Baltica and Siberia form a hairpin
shapes and the length of these hairpins match, but the age of their apexes
do not. We regard that this may be due to lack of coeval data and pro-
pose that the oscillation along the same great circle path indicate TPW
